primitives.name: Observation Representation
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model - Observations (3 representations): Pixels (1280×720 RGB), Super Mini Map (4 binary 72×96 matrices: home/away/ball/active player; stackable across timesteps), Floats (115-dim compact vector: coordinates, possession, direction, game mode).
primitives.assumptions: Observations are conditionally independent given the current game state; each representation encodes distinct aspects of the environment.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At game start or after reset, all representations are initialized to zero or default values.

layer2.mapping: Each observation type maps to a GSI state vector via a learned embedding function, enabling unified probabilistic inference.
layer2.telemetry: Mean squared error between predicted and actual observation sequences.

primitives.name: Action Space
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Actions (19): 8 movement directions, short/high/long pass, shot, slide tackle, dribble, sprint, stop-dribble, stop-moving, stop-sprint, do-nothing.
primitives.assumptions: Actions are executed atomically and influence the next game state deterministically under physics simulation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When agent is out-of-bounds or in offside position, certain actions are invalid or penalized.

layer2.mapping: Action space is embedded into GSE’s policy kernel as a discrete stochastic transition operator over state-action pairs.
layer2.telemetry: Entropy of action distribution across episodes.

primitives.name: Difficulty Parameterization
primitives.verbatim_quote: Rule-based opponent bot with difficulty θ ∈ [0,1] (easy 0.05, medium 0.6, hard 0.95).
primitives.assumptions: Opponent bot reaction time scales inversely with θ; higher θ implies more reactive behavior.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At θ = 0, bot acts randomly; at θ = 1, bot behaves optimally.

layer2.mapping: θ maps to a GSI adversarial strength prior, used in Bayesian updating of opponent behavior models.
layer2.telemetry: Average reward difference between agent and opponent across difficulty levels.

primitives.name: Reward Shaping
primitives.verbatim_quote: Key quantitative definitions: checkpoint reward +0.1 × 10 regions; difficulty θ parameterization via bot reaction-time scaling; game length 3000 frames default / 400 frames for Academy scenarios (ending on score, ball loss, or stoppage).
primitives.assumptions: Checkpoint rewards encourage spatial exploration; sparse scoring rewards are secondary.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At terminal states (goal, ball loss), reward is adjusted based on final outcome.

layer2.mapping: Reward structure is encoded in GSE’s value function approximation as a weighted sum of temporal difference errors.
layer2.telemetry: Cumulative reward variance across training episodes.

reasoning_traces.think:
The Google Research Football (GRF) environment is designed as a reinforcement learning benchmark with a 3D physics-based soccer simulation. It supports multi-agent self-play and is computationally accessible, addressing the core research question of building a challenging yet tractable RL environment. The environment uses three observation types—pixels, super mini map (SMM), and float vectors—to represent the game state. These are mapped into a unified state space for policy learning. The action space consists of 19 discrete actions including movement, passing, shooting, and physical interactions. The difficulty of the opponent is controlled by a scalar parameter θ, which modulates bot reaction time. Reward shaping includes checkpoint rewards for progressing through defined regions, encouraging exploration. The environment supports both stochastic and deterministic modes. Benchmarks include 3 difficulty levels, 2 reward schemes, 3 algorithms, and 5 seeds, evaluated via mean average goal difference with confidence intervals. Academy scenarios provide curriculum learning tasks. The key mathematical abstraction is that GRF models a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) where the agent must infer hidden states from noisy observations and act under uncertainty. The failure modes arise from limited generalization to real-world football due to its simplified dynamics and lack of complex tactical structures.
